catalog_quote: Vowel length is distinctive in accented syllables (nánande ‘heart’ vs. nánde ‘inside wall’), but this contrast was not recognized by linguists until the 1990s and is still marked only sporadically in written materials. ... A downstep pitch accent occurs on the first or second syllable of the word, and is distinctive: watháthe ‘food’ wáthathe ‘table’, though this may turn out to correlate with vowel length. Instrumental phonetic studies of O-P are lacking. It would be useful to have studies of the exact quality of the various stop series, th, and the suprasegmental features.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Rudin & Shea 2005 quotation is verbatim on p. 3 of the held postprint, and the Marsault 2021 corroborating quotations (sec. 2.2.3 p. 98, fn. 16; sec. 3.5.1) are verbatim in the held thesis. (2) Deciding source is a short specialist encyclopedia sketch (2005) backed by a 2021 dissertation grammar sketch that relays the only dedicated accent work (Koontz 1988, Larson 2009, both unpublished SCLC papers). Both sources agree: culminative pitch ('downstep pitch') accent, lexically contrastive position within a left-edge two-syllable window, leftward shift under prefixation — matching the catalog's TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT / lexical-within-window coding. Both sources state that instrumental/prosodic documentation is lacking, so no better instrumental source is known; Brave/DDG/Mojeek/OpenAlex/S2 rate-limite
